body.heading: Your skin measures flow, not temperature
paragraphs: Leave a metal railing and a wooden bench side by side on a cold morning and both settle to exactly the same temperature. Yet the railing feels bitterly cold and the bench merely cool. A thermometer says your senses are lying — in fact, your senses are measuring something different from temperature.

Skin does not detect how hot an object is; it detects how fast heat is flowing out of (or into) your hand. A fast flow reads as intense cold or intense heat. A slow flow reads as mild, whatever the actual temperature of the object may be.

body.heading: Metal is a heat highway, wood is a country lane
paragraphs: Metal conducts heat superbly. The instant your warm hand touches cold metal, heat rushes out of your skin into the railing, and keeps rushing, because the metal carries it away into the whole structure. Your skin cools fast, and your nerves report: very cold.

Wood is a poor conductor — an insulator. Heat leaves your hand slowly, and the thin surface layer of the wood warms up to nearly skin temperature within moments. With the flow reduced to a trickle, the bench feels almost neutral, though it started at exactly the railing's temperature.

body.heading: The same trick, all over the house
paragraphs: Step out of a shower onto a tiled floor and then onto a bath mat: same room, same temperature, same illusion in reverse roles. The tiles conduct heat from your feet quickly and feel cold; the mat insulates and feels warm. Carpet over concrete works the same way all winter.

The effect also explains why a metal spoon in hot soup becomes dangerous while a wooden spoon stays comfortable, and why steel playground slides can feel scorching in summer sun: metal does not get hotter than the wood beside it — it just hands the heat to you much faster.
